key_facts: Malignant tumour of **melanocytes**; the UK's fifth commonest cancer (about 17,500 cases a year).
Risk: **UV and sunburn**, sunbeds, many or atypical naevi, fair skin, family history, previous melanoma, immunosuppression.
Recognise with the **ABCDE** rule, the NICE **7-point checklist** and the **ugly duckling** sign; nodular melanoma may be EFG (elevated, firm, growing).
Refer any suspicious pigmented lesion on the **suspected cancer pathway** (NICE NG12); never destroy an undiagnosed pigmented lesion.
Prognosis depends mostly on **Breslow thickness** at diagnosis.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Melanoma is a malignant tumour of melanocytes. In the UK it is the **5th commonest cancer** (about 17,500–20,000 new cases a year), with rising incidence, especially in people over 65. It is one of the commonest cancers in young adults (15–34).
Subtypes describe the growth pattern. **Breslow thickness, not subtype, drives stage and prognosis.**

sub: About **17,500** new cases a year in the UK; incidence has more than doubled since the 1990s.
One of the commonest cancers in **15–34-year-olds**; median age at diagnosis in the mid-60s.
Men: trunk (back) most common; women: legs.
Acral lentiginous melanoma (palms, soles, nails) is the commonest type in people with dark skin.

ul: **Intermittent intense UV and sunburn** (especially in childhood), sunbeds, fair skin (MC1R), many or atypical naevi, family history, previous melanoma, and immunosuppression.

**Driver mutations:** **BRAF V600** in ~40–50% (intermittently sun-exposed skin). This is the target for BRAF/MEK inhibitors; NRAS ~20%; NF1 (chronically sun-damaged skin, desmoplastic); **KIT** in acral/mucosal/CSD melanomas (the course c-KIT)
Growth phases: radial (in situ / thin), then vertical (nodular, invasive). Breslow thickness tracks the vertical phase.
**UV exposure**: intermittent intense exposure and **sunburn** (especially in childhood), sunbed use.
**Host**: many naevi (over 100), atypical naevi, fair skin type I–II, red hair, freckling.
**Genetic**: family history (CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1, MC1R variants), previous melanoma, immunosuppression, giant congenital naevus.
**"Melanoma is always dark and irregular"**: amelanotic and nodular melanomas can be pink and symmetrical.
**"Dark skin doesn't get melanoma"**: acral and nail melanomas occur and are often diagnosed late.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Melanoma arises when **melanocytes** accumulate mutations that switch on growth and switch off brakes.

mech.t: UV-signature mutations activate the **MAPK pathway** (BRAF V600E in about half, NRAS) and inactivate tumour suppressors (CDKN2A, PTEN, TP53).
Most melanomas first spread sideways within the epidermis (superficial spreading, lentigo maligna), when cure by excision is very likely.
mech.caption: Superficial spreading melanoma (radial growth along the epidermis) vs nodular melanoma (early vertical growth into the dermis).

mech.t: Cells invade the dermis; deeper tumours (thicker **Breslow**) have greater metastatic risk. Nodular melanoma enters this phase early.
Tumours evade T cells (e.g. via PD-L1), the basis for immunotherapy.
Spread to lymph nodes, skin, lung, liver and brain.

histo: Atypical melanocytes in nests and single cells at all levels of the epidermis (**pagetoid spread**), with asymmetry and poor circumscription.
Report includes **Breslow thickness**, ulceration, mitoses and margins, which guide AJCC staging and treatment.

sub: Look at **palms, soles and nails**: acral lentiginous melanoma and nail melanoma (Hutchinson sign) present late.
Naevi can darken in pregnancy, but a changing lesion still needs assessment; melanoma is rare in children (Spitz-like lesions need specialist review).

ul: **Diagnostic accuracy by eye** rises with experience. The course figures (consultant ~80%, registrar 50–60%, GP ~40%) are in line with older studies, but published estimates vary widely.

**Dermoscopy** improves accuracy in trained users: meta-analyses show sensitivity rising from about 70% to about 90%, with an odds ratio of ~15 for diagnostic accuracy versus the naked eye. **Untrained use may not help.**

**Dermoscopic melanoma features:** atypical network; irregular streaks / pseudopods; irregular dots and globules; **blue-white veil**; regression structures; negative network; shiny white lines; atypical (polymorphous/dotted) vessels; acral **parallel-ridge** pattern; facial LM: asymmetric follicular openings, rhomboid structures, annular-granular pattern; Algorithms: **3-point checklist** (asymmetry, atypical network, blue-white structures; ≥2 = refer), 7-point dermoscopic checklist, ABCD rule (Stolz), CASH, TADA, "chaos and clues"

**Training and simulators:** PCDS dermoscopy courses, the BAD/BDNG, International Dermoscopy Society (dermoscopy-ids.org) online tutorials, DermNet's dermoscopy course, and image-based simulators (e.g. "Dermoscopedia", quiz banks). The evidence supports structured training with regular practice and feedback.

**AI and algorithms:** **NICE HTG746** (formerly HTE24) supports *conditional* NHS use of **DERM** (Skin Analytics) to triage lesions **already referred** on the urgent skin cancer pathway, with dermatologist oversight. Images of black or brown skin (Fitzpatrick V–VI) still need human review. Consumer apps are mostly unregulated. **An app result never overrides clinical concern** in either direction.

ddx.f: Red, bleeds; but amelanotic melanoma mimics PG.

ddx.f: Trauma, grows out; no fold pigment.

ddx.f: Uniform flat brown on sun-damaged skin.

blocks: SK (the [benign lesion](condition:seborrhoeic-keratosis) notes see *Biopsy, Breslow thickness and the histopathology report*; ), atypical naevus, pigmented BCC, DF, angiokeratoma (the [skin lumps](condition:dermatofibroma) notes see *Immunotherapy and targeted therapy: what the IP must know*), haemangioma/thrombosed angioma, pyogenic granuloma (amelanotic nodular melanoma mimic; ), subungual haematoma (nail), acral naevus, lentigo/flat SK (vs LM), and metastasis.

As in *Recognition, diagnostic accuracy, dermoscopy and AI*. LM vs solar lentigo/flat SK (dermoscopy, biopsy). ALM vs acral naevus, haematoma (talon noir, "black heel"), wart, and fungal (tinea nigra).

ul: **Suspected cancer pathway referral (2WW)** if: the 7-point score is ≥3; dermoscopy suggests melanoma; or; a nodule fits EFG (nodular melanoma)
**Make the referral within 1 working day** of deciding. Include dermoscopic/clinical images if a teledermatology triage route exists (see *Teledermatology*).
Document size (ruler), duration, change, the 7-point score, and safety-netting.
**Do not:** freeze, shave, laser or "watch and wait" on a lesion meeting criteria; or reassure because an app is negative.
Previous **repeated reassurance** is a classic **diagnostic-delay pattern**. When a patient re-presents with persistent concern, take it seriously, and consider reporting it as a learning event.

**Check soles, palms and nails** in every skin of colour presentation, and **do not label a pigmented sole lesion as a "bruise" or "verruca"** without follow-up. Subungual: Hutchinson's sign → suspected cancer pathway (the [nail disorders](condition:paronychia) notes).
LM on the face of an older person: an elderly red flag (the [older skin pages](condition:itch-xerosis-older-adults) notes quick reference), so use the suspected cancer pathway.

blocks.h: Case 1: 54-year-old, nodule >12 months, repeatedly reassured; an app flagged it

ul: **Diagnosis:** nodular melanoma (EFG: elevated, firm, growing).
**Action:** **NG12 suspected cancer pathway** (1.7.1 score ≥3 and/or 1.7.3 nodular melanoma), referral within 1 working day.
**Excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin** (the course "narrow margin") by the skin cancer team, then WLE per Breslow.
**Diagnostic accuracy:** consultants ~80%, registrars 50–60%, GPs ~40% (course teaching; study-dependent); dermoscopy adds about 10–20% in trained hands.
**Learning points:** repeated reassurance = diagnostic delay; an app is not a diagnostic tool, but a flag deserves clinical review.

blocks.h: Case 2: 17-year-old of Irish ancestry, >50 atypical moles, father and grandfather with melanoma in their 30s, other family cancers

ul: **Diagnosis:** FAMMM (familial atypical multiple mole melanoma) syndrome.
**Gene:** **CDKN2A** (p16). Also consider CDK4, BAP1 and MC1R modifiers.
**Associated cancer:** **pancreatic adenocarcinoma**.
**Plan:** dermatology surveillance (total-body photography plus digital dermoscopy), clinical genetics, sun protection, no sunbeds (under-18 law), self-examination, no smoking.

blocks.h: Case 3: 30-year-old, lesion changing over 2 years, teledermatology images

ul: **Pathway:** 2WW with images → excision biopsy (2 mm) → WLE.
**Pathology:** Breslow **1.4 mm** (depth, not 1.5 cm diameter), **ulcerated** → **T2b**.
**Stage:** **IIA** if node-negative; SLNB decides (if positive → IIIA or higher).
**5-year MSS:** ~93–94% (AJCC 8), not ~80%. Mitoses >5/mm² are prognostic only, not staging.
**WLE:** **2 cm margin** (stage II, NG14).
**SLNB:** **consider/discuss** (Breslow >1 mm).
**Imaging:** not required at IIA (consider at IIB).
**Adjuvant:** none at IIA (pembrolizumab TA837 is for IIB/IIC).
**Follow-up:** 3-monthly for 3 years, then 6-monthly to 5 years. Self-examination; vitamin D measured at diagnosis.

ladder.t: **Suspected cancer pathway** (NG12 1.7.1 score ≥ 3; 1.7.3 nodular) **within 1 working day**. Include images if teledermatology triage exists; document the score and safety-net.
**Excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin** by the skin cancer team → WLE per Breslow.
Sun protection, no sunbeds; full-skin self-checks; first-degree relatives ~2× risk. Many atypical moles + family melanoma: consider **FAMMM / CDKN2A** (pancreatic cancer link) → genetics.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Don’t**: Freeze, shave, laser or ‘watch and wait’ a lesion meeting criteria; reassure because an app is negative.
**Pigmented ‘verruca’ or ‘bruise’ on the sole**: Refer if not resolving; not more destructive treatment.

refer.t: 7-point score **≥ 3** or dermoscopy suggesting melanoma: suspected cancer pathway.
**Firm growing nodule > 1 month** (EFG), even if pink or symmetrical.
New growing dark mark on sole, palm or nail; Hutchinson’s sign.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: NICE weighted 7-point checklist score **3 or more**, or dermoscopy suggesting melanoma: **suspected cancer pathway** referral (NG12 1.7.1–1.7.3).
A firm, growing nodule over a month (EFG), even if pink or symmetrical: suspected **nodular melanoma**.
A new dark mark on the sole, palm or nail that is growing: suspected **acral melanoma** (check the nail fold for Hutchinson’s sign).
Local recurrence, in-transit metastases.
Lymph node and distant metastasis.
Treatment toxicity (immunotherapy immune-related adverse events).
Five-year survival is over **95%** for thin (stage I) melanoma, falling with thickness and spread.
Further primary melanomas occur in about 5–10%: lifelong skin self-checks.

pearls: "Any spot that is raised, firm and growing, of any colour, needs to be seen within two weeks."
Sun-protection counselling and full-skin self-checks for family members (first-degree relatives have about twice the risk).
A "verruca" that doesn't respond to salicylic acid or cryo and is pigmented or bleeding needs referral, not more destructive treatment.
